items.title: Refugee families use agroforestry to restore degraded landscape in Bangladesh camp
items.summary: KUTUPALONG REFUGEE CAMP, Bangladesh —”It is like a jail, but it isn’t a jail,” says Roshid Ahamed Bin, a 47-year-old Rohingya farmer, living in what is now a refugee camp in Bangladesh. It is far from the farmland where he used to live in Myanmar, before he and thousands of Rohingya people like him fled persecution eight years ago. Here, amid the world’s largest refugee settlement with over 1.1 million refugees, space is tight and evergreen forests have paid the price. But families are combining NGO-funded farming projects with traditional Rohingya agroecology techniques to create agroforestry plots that are restoring land while helping refugees become self-sufficient in response to deep cuts in international food aid. “I feel so bad here as I have no land, but I am keeping my ancestors’ heritage alive. Growing these crops reminds me of the life we had in Myanmar. Here, life is difficult,” said Amina Khatun, a 58-year-old refugee living in Camp 1W, a sector of the sprawling settlement. Before the 2017 influx, Kutupalong refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar was a tropical evergreen forest, dominated by Dipterocarpus species, and sanctuary for endangered Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). To make way for the massive refugee settlements, the Bangladeshi government allocated roughly 2,500 hectares (6,100 acres) of protected forest land, and refugees and aid agencies cleared the vegetation to build shelters and provide firewood. Over 1,500 hectares of forest were cleared in total. The rain, with nowhere to soak in, ran straight down the slopes. Landslides became…This article was…
items.t: Refugee families use agroforestry to restore degraded landscape in Bangladesh camp

items.title: In Republic of Congo, residents and a scientist take on a fight against lead pollution
items.summary: Nearly 120 residents of Vindoulou, a neighborhood in Pointe-Noire, Republic of Congo, have filed a civil claim before the city’s High Court in relation to pollution allegedly caused by a foundry. “We want tests, but also compensation for damages and losses,” Cyrille Traoré Ndembi, a plaintiff and president of the Vindoulou Residents’ Collective, which represents people living in the working-class neighborhood, told Mongabay on the phone. The civil case, filed in October, is the latest in a series of actions taken against Metssa Congo, a foundry that opened in the neighborhood in 2013.The facility recycled, among other things, car batteries, extracting lead and turning it into lead bars for export. The plant is part of the Metssa Group, an industrial metals trading company based in the United Arab Emirates. The battery recycling process can pose serious health risks. According to the WHO, lead can be released in the form of fumes, particles and dust at every stage of the process, from draining and dismantling to smelting and refining. Environmental contamination from recycling can be substantial, exposing workers and nearby communities to significant levels of lead, the health agency says on its website. According to Traore Ndembi, residents of Vindoulou soon experienced this reality first-hand, complaining about toxic fumes coming from the plant. In 2019, they decided to register their discontent over pollution. “We wrote to the public authorities, to the departmental director of health,” Traoré Ndembi said. “We also wrote to the local environmental authorities but they…
items.t: In Republic of Congo, residents and a scientist take on a fight against lead pollution

items.title: What kind of wealth do Borneo’s ancient rainforests hold?
items.summary: What kind of wealth do Borneo’s ancient rainforests hold? Industries such as logging and palm oil have generated vast monetary wealth for some. But for the Indigenous communities who call the Malaysian Borneo home—its forests, rivers and mountains hold a different kind of value. These forests are interconnected ecosystems that sustain communities with food, medicine and livelihoods, while holding generations of knowledge, traditions and culture. But as industrial pressures continue to pressure these landscapes, some communities are working harder than ever to defend their homes and protect the ecological wealth that exists in these forests. Special thanks to Celine Lim, Boyce Ngau Anyie and @TheBorneoProjectThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: What kind of wealth do Borneo’s ancient rainforests hold?

items.title: Aerial photos show recovery of Florida Bay, US, as restoration sends Everglades water
items.summary: Freshwater flows into Florida Bay, significantly reduced by decades of Everglades drainage, are slowly increasing under the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan. Helicopter surveys by avian ecologist Mark Ian Cook document returning wading birds, wintering waterfowl, American flamingos and threatened American crocodiles. Wading bird nesting reached a record high in 2018 but has since declined, while a severe 2025–2026 drought underscored the birds’ sensitivity to water fluctuations. From a low-flying helicopter above the coastal Everglades in southern Florida, U.S., Mark Ian Cook looks down at dense mangrove forests and silty shallows rarely seen by others. Below him, bottlenose dolphins trap mullet in rings of mud, nurse sharks mate in sheltered waters and flamingos forage on remote mudflats. Mating Nurse Sharks. Two nurse sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum) mate off Shark Point in Everglades National Park. Unlike bony fish, sharks must make physical contact to reproduce: The male grips the female’s pectoral fin in his mouth to hold position. Image by Mark Ian Cook. Cook, an avian ecologist who heads the South Florida Water Management District’s Everglades Research Group, tracks how wading birds respond to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP), a decades-long federal-state effort to return freshwater to the southern Everglades and Florida Bay. He conducts a flying survey about every two weeks during the birds’ breeding season, photographing nesting colonies through a small flap in the helicopter door. Some colonies hold tens of thousands of nests, too many…
items.t: Aerial photos show recovery of Florida Bay, US, as restoration sends Everglades water

items.title: ‘Vote for trees’: Taiwan community pins hope on ‘Forest Grandma’ to save beloved woods
items.summary: KAOHSIUNG, Taiwan — At dawn, just as the birds begin to sing, Chiang Huang-nu usually puts on her traditional straw hat and walks through the wooded grounds of a former sugar factory in Ciaotou district in southwest Taiwan. Along the way, the 83-year-old might greet around 30 other regular strollers, most of them retirees. Chiang has taken these morning walks among the greenery since she was a child. For the past several months, the walk has involved chatting with fellow community members about the community’s fight against the government’s plan to redevelop the area and demolish their beloved wood. For decades, Chiang and fellow residents have spent their mornings in the Ciaotou Woodland, a 154-hectare (380-acre) urban forest surrounding the historic Ciaotou Sugar Refinery. Located in the eponymous district, north of Kaohsiung city center in southwestern Taiwan, the woodland is home to 100,000 trees, according to local environmentalists, and a habitat for local wildlife. “Some of the trees were planted during the Japanese colonial period,” which lasted from 1895 to 1945, Chiang told Mongabay. “They are more than 100 years old. They protect us from the heat in summer.” For the past year, however, residents can only walk in the nearby park. The woodland has been fenced off and made inaccessible to the public, following a government order. Its trees are under threat from the urban redevelopment project. On a November morning, three elderly men in their 70s were sitting on plastic chairs in the middle of the park, sheltered…This article was originally published on…
items.t: ‘Vote for trees’: Taiwan community pins hope on ‘Forest Grandma’ to save beloved woods

items.title: Bigfoot enthusiasts hope government’s US sightings files are ‘just the beginning’ of proving the creature real
items.summary:
The Forest Service’s work will ‘help normalize’ talk happening ‘for decades’, says ‘wood ape’ conservancy director

When the Forest Service, one of the US government’s less sexy departments, quietly posted three documents to its website in mid-October, it was probably hoping to avoid a fuss.

It didn’t succeed. The files were about Bigfoot, after all, and their publication sparked interest from around the globe, with Bigfoot enthusiasts hopeful that this could be a key step step in the road to proving the creature is real.

items.title: A tiny deep-sea fish eaten 42 years ago has now been named a new species
items.summary: A new-to-science species of deep-sea fish has been described from a single specimen found in the stomach contents of a predatory fish that ate it in 1984. The specimen sat in a Tokyo museum collection for 42 years until it was examined by museum staff and volunteers. The newly described deepwater cardinalfish (Epigonus masamunei) has large eyes, which is common for fish that live in the dark waters of the deep sea, and measures about 8 centimeters (3 inches) from snout to tail base. The species’ name comes from Masamune, a medieval Japanese swordsmith, because the curve of its spine resembles the swords he made. “I was extremely excited,” Makoto Okamoto, the study’s author and a fish taxonomist at the Japan Fisheries Research and Education Agency, told Mongabay by email. “The moment of discovering a new species is always fresh and thrilling.” No one has ever seen the species alive, and so no one knows what color it is either, Okamoto said. The predator was a beardfish (Polymixia japonica), another, larger, deep-sea fish that commonly grows to about 20 cm (8 in) long. In July 1984, a research vessel caught the beardfish at an estimated depth of 370-450 meters (1,210-1,480 feet) off Kita-iwo Island, in Japan’s Ogasawara Islands in the western Pacific Ocean, according to museum records cited in the study. The beardfish may have vomited the cardinalfish back up, as the specimen’s belly, skin and the tips of some fin spines were damaged. “It is rare for new species…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: A tiny deep-sea fish eaten 42 years ago has now been named a new species

items.title: This Dog Has Been Bringing His Lookalike Toy Everywhere For Years, And It’s The Sweetest Friendship (36 Pics)
items.summary:
Most dog toys don’t last long. They get chewed, torn open, buried in the garden or replaced with something new. Shrimp is the exception. Since 2017, this plush has belonged to Gumbo, a golden retriever mix who looks so much like his stuffed companion that the two could pass for brothers.

Gumbo’s story began with a career that never quite took off. Hana Brickman was studying nursing at Washington State University when she volunteered to train service dogs and was matched with him as a puppy. He didn’t make the cut. In her words, he was “not serious enough” for the job, so she adopted him. Years later, at her local IKEA in Vancouver, Washington, she spotted a soft toy that looked strikingly like him and bought it for herself. Gumbo had other plans.

He began carrying it everywhere, proudly showing it off to guests at home and to strangers on the trail. Hana let her Instagram followers pick a name, “Shrimp” won the vote, and she has been documenting the pair’s adventures ever since. We’ve gathered some of the most heartwarming photos of this inseparable duo, celebrating a friendship that has stood the test of time. Scroll down to see them, and let us know in the comments which one is your favorite!

More info: Instagram 

#1 © Photo: mycaninelife 

Over the years, Shrimp has seen more of the world than most plush toys ever will. He has climbed mountains, camped on beaches, flown on planes and crossed the US on long road trips. He has posed in colorful flower fields, hiked in Canada and Arizona, visited Disney, and one Halloween even wore a ghost costume to match his best…
items.t: This Dog Has Been Bringing His Lookalike Toy Everywhere For Years, And It’s The Sweetest Friendship (36 Pics)

items.title: Whales return to Patagonia, but face new threats in Argentina
items.summary: Whales are coming back to Argentina’s coast. Decades after commercial hunting decimated their populations, different species of cetaceans are once again repopulating parts of the Argentine Sea. Scientists are now monitoring this recovery through new sightings and technologies that track their migratory routes and feeding grounds. While the growing whale population offers an encouraging sign for marine conservation, climate change, krill fishing and expanding oil and gas development pose new challenges to their survival. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) have returned to the Beagle Channel in Argentina’s far south to feed in waters where their sightings had been declining for decades. A local initiative has identified 208 individuals since 2013 and documented a steady rise in sightings since at least 2018. Among the recorded whales are a female called Shima, who returned to the channel for eight consecutive years, and a young male called Buddha, spotted again after several years without any sightings. Researchers say this return may reflect a broader recovery of cetacean populations following decades-old bans on commercial whaling. In 2025, a collaborative analysis identified 22 humpback whales in the channel, 17 of them recorded for the first time. The project relied on photographs submitted by boat crews, tour guides, photographers and tourists. The unique markings on their tail flukes allows researchers to distinguish between individuals. The animals enter these waters searching for food, feeding primarily on squat lobster (Munida gregaria) and Falkland sprat…
items.t: Whales return to Patagonia, but face new threats in Argentina

items.title: Zambian court again delays copper miner’s bid to block pollution lawsuit
items.summary: Zambia’s top court has postponed for the fourth time an appeal by copper miner Sino Metals, which is trying to block a lawsuit against it from proceeding. The latest adjournment comes amid ongoing concerns over disputed resettlement offers. In February 2025, the dam holding the mining waste at the Sino Metals Leach Zambia Limited mine near the community of Kalusale, in Copperbelt province, collapsed. This released millions of liters of acidic mining waste, contaminating soils, crops, and waterways connected to the Kafue River system, which millions of Zambians rely on. In response, 176 people from Kalusale and Chambishi filed a constitutional petition in the Lusaka High Court in September 2025, seeking compensation for the damage caused by the spill. They also demanded environmental restoration and support for affected households, arguing their constitutional rights had been violated. Sino Metals appealed to the court to have the petition thrown out, arguing that a constitutional petition was not the correct legal procedure to bring the claim. It asserted that Zambia’s Bill of Rights does not apply to private corporations, only to the state. The High Court dismissed these objections, so Sino Metals took its appeal to the Supreme Court. While hearing the company’s appeal in June 2026, the Supreme Court allowed the Zambian government to join the case as the matter affected the wider public. The latest Supreme Court adjournment, on Nov. 18, follows an affidavit submitted by Attorney General Mulilo Dimas Kabesha, who asked the court to give the parties additional…
items.t: Zambian court again delays copper miner’s bid to block pollution lawsuit

items.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
items.summary: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.
items.t: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

items.title: This Photographer Captures The Fascinating Lives Of Birds In 41 Stunning Images
items.summary:
A hummingbird stopping for a fraction of a second to feed, a toucan taking off from a branch, or a bird wrestling with its prey are all moments that Colombian wildlife photographer Luis Fernando Serna Agudelo sets out to capture. Getting these shots, however, often takes hours, if not days, of observing birds and learning their habits.

Luis Fernando’s interest in wildlife dates back to his childhood, when he spent school vacations at his grandmother’s coffee farm in Alejandría, Colombia. At 18, he began working on a wildlife documentary series, which introduced him to the challenges of photographing birds and eventually led him to develop a particular interest in them. While he certainly appreciates the striking colors and unusual features of the birds he encounters, he is equally interested in what they do. His photographs offer a closer look at how birds hunt, feed, interact with one another, and live in the wild.

Bored Panda reached out to Luis Fernando to learn more about his work, the challenges of photographing birds in flight, and some of his most memorable encounters in the wild. Scroll down to enjoy a selection of his photographs and read what he shared with us!

items.t: This Photographer Captures The Fascinating Lives Of Birds In 41 Stunning Images

items.title: Meet the few Liberian women rangers in a race to protect wildlife and forests
items.summary: ZORTAPA, Liberia — Grace Kotee-Zansi is living a dream she had as a child: patrolling the East Nimba Nature Reserve (ENNR) as a biologist ranger to stop hunters from killing protected animals. Her job today brings relief from her childhood memories of her grandfather hunting and farming in the forest. The ENNR, a proposed extension to a UNESCO World Heritage Site, covers 13,500 hectares (33,400 acres). Zansi says she’s working to stop wildlife killing and tree cutting. She patrols the forest, checking cameras installed to capture animals and human activities. The Mount Nimba landscape lost roughly 9.9% of its total forest cover between 2013 and 2020, according to a report using satellite imagery. Zansi is one of the few women serving as a ranger here, making her stand out in a field dominated by men. For decades, men have carried out forest protection in Liberia, with only a few women like Zansi now joining the race. They patrol for months, leaving their spouses and children at home, tracking poachers, documenting animal footprints and recording illegal human activity in the park. Official data from the Liberian Forestry Development Authority (FDA) state that a total of 143 rangers are deployed across Liberia’s protected areas; only 17 are women. This gap is due to the struggle of “recruiting qualified women who are willing and prepared to serve as rangers,” the FDA tells Mongabay. “Liberia’s ranger workforce continues to expand through various biodiversity conservation initiatives. However, comprehensive gender-disaggregated data remain limited, and available…
items.t: Meet the few Liberian women rangers in a race to protect wildlife and forests

items.title: Hong Kong becomes key link in illegal trade of Australia’s native reptiles
items.summary: From lizards to snakes, Hong Kong is emerging as a primary trafficking center for native Australian reptiles, reports contributor Selina Cheng for Mongabay. In December 2025, customs authorities intercepted a consignment from Australia containing 13 live lizards stuffed inside winter boots. Hong Kong’s customs agency said the air cargo was falsely declared as snacks. This was the fourth such seizure of live native Australian reptiles by Hong Kong customs authorities between 2025 and 2026. Across the four seizures, officials confiscated at least 98 animals, including 74 lizards and 24 snakes, valued at more than HK$1.1 million ($141,100). Intelligence briefing papers from researchers at the Wildlife Crime Research Hub at Adelaide University in Australia confirmed that Hong Kong “functions both as a destination and a potential transit hub within broader trafficking networks.” In Australia, keeping native reptiles as pets is strictly regulated and requires a license. But Hong Kong and mainland China don’t require proof of legal origin or documentation for possession. This has allowed illegally smuggled wildlife to be “laundered” in Hong Kong’s legal trade. Australia has since 1982 also banned commercial exports of live native species. However, an estimated 15% of Australia’s endemic reptile species have entered illicit international trade, according to the Wildlife Crime Research Hub. Dylan Chadwick, from the research hub, told Mongabay that demand is high for skinks in the genus Tiliqua, including the shingleback (Tiliqua rugosa), nicknamed the “pine cone lizard” in China.…
items.t: Hong Kong becomes key link in illegal trade of Australia’s native reptiles

items.title: Sri Lanka deploys ‘elephant army’ to protect rare tuskers, but experts urge caution
items.summary: A beloved male elephant named Kavantissa that frequented a rural village in Sri Lanka recently died from a gunshot injury, sparking public outrage. Environmentalists condemned authorities for what they called a “lack of care” for this iconic elephant, while local animal rights groups demanded an independent investigation into the death. In response, the Sri Lankan government launched a military operation called Hasthi Sena, which translates to an “elephant army,” reports contributor Malaka Rodrigo for Mongabay. This task force brings together some 100 members from Sri Lanka’s armed forces and departments of wildlife and civil defense. Its goal is to prevent further elephant killings, curb wildlife crime, and bolster surveillance across hotspots of human-elephant encounters. As of early November, the task force had already arrested individuals involved in illegal activities such as setting wire snares and using trap guns. Since Kavantissa’s death, public support for assigning armed personnel to elephants with large tusks. Such tuskers, as they’re known are rare among Asian elephants (Elephas maximus). In Sri Lanka, a 1999 study estimated that only about 7.5% of male elephants are tuskers. Over the past 10 years, advocacy group Wild Tuskers Srilanka (WTS) has documented 300 such elephants. The group also recently identified 17 tuskers as being at high risk and needing urgent monitoring, in part due to the overlap of their ranges with human settlements, said Chandika Lakshan, a WTS member. The organization has handed over the detailed profiles of the 17 tuskers to government…
items.t: Sri Lanka deploys ‘elephant army’ to protect rare tuskers, but experts urge caution

items.title: In Nepal, experts debate future of mega-dams after August’s flood
items.summary: KATHMANDU — Until recently, residents living in the lap of the Himalayas saw the peaks as immovable giants silently nurturing them with snowmelt. But on Aug. 26, there was a road from the mountain overlooking the Bhotekoshi rivershed in central Nepal roared. What appears to have been an avalanche on Langtang Lirung sent a churning wall of water, mud and boulders down the valley. In Nepal, more than 1,353 people were killed and many thousands went missing. The flood also damaged at least a dozen hydropower projects. As the flood receded, a debate surfaced in Nepal’s policy circles about the future of hydropower. Some experts now advocate mega-dams in the Himalayas to contain large floods, manage winter power shortages and even prepare for a future without snow in the Himalaya. But limits to engineering and earthquakes in the young mountains challenge any such endeavor, experts tell Mongabay. “The question for the future is not whether Nepal will continue to develop its rivers,” writes David Fickling, climate and energy columnist for Bloomberg. “It is whether the next generation of hydro projects merely extracts electricity with run-of-river, or builds storage dams to give downstream communities greater protection against the consequences of our increasingly deadly climate.” Reservoir dams, which store large volumes of water and generate electricity on demand, have long been part of government policy. The pro-dam camp points to Kulekhani, located southwest of Kathmandu, which generates 92 GWh (Gigawatt-hour) annually and helps meet winter peak demand. But the four-decade-old…
items.t: In Nepal, experts debate future of mega-dams after August’s flood

items.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
items.summary: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.
items.t: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean

items.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
items.summary: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.
items.t: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years

items.title: Community forests offer hope for conservation in DRC, but major hurdles remain
items.summary: LUBUMBASHI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an initiative is underway to award community-based forestry land titles to 7.1 million hectares of land, or about 17.5 million acres — an area the size of Ireland. This is one of several conservation strategies aimed at protecting the DRC’s biodiversity while recognizing customary rights over the land. Apart from the protected areas that have been formally established to date and the vast Kivu-Kinshasa green corridor, the number of local community forest concessions (CFCLs) has risen from eight in 2017 to more than 350 in 2026, of which at least 236 have been legally established. However, while they provide the legal framework that protects communities from unjust or arbitrary expropriation, and allow certain communities to benefit from their forests, CFCLs also have the task of creating opportunities for communities. Without these opportunities, some communities are tempted to illegally exploit their own forests. One decade after the ministerial decree that established the rules for managing and operating these concessions, Mongabay’s Didier Makal speaks with two experts in the sector to get their take on progress. Official presentation of forest concession titles from local communities (CFCL) to the members of the community of Bafwalungu (territory of Bafwasende). Image courtesy of Tropenbos. Blaise Mudodosi, a doctoral researcher at the University of Goma in the DRC, works on the implementation and evaluation of community forestry projects and serves as the national coordinator of the NGO…
items.t: Community forests offer hope for conservation in DRC, but major hurdles remain

items.title: ‘Disaster’ unfolding as Sydney fire ant outbreak partly blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations
items.summary:
Farmers’ Federation president says Australia ‘can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country … let alone some of these difficult-to-detect pests’

Years-old recommendations by Australia’s biosecurity watchdog have been ignored or not acted on by successive federal governments, increasing the risk of an invasive pest outbreak such as the fire ants discovered in Sydney this week, according to experts.

Environmentalists and biosecurity experts warn the large colony of red imported fire ants is a warning sign that the country’s quarantine system is too slow-moving, underfunded and overly concerned with agriculture.

items.title: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels
items.summary: On Nov. 19, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that aims to speed up permitting for energy infrastructure projects. The 62-33 vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) included support from pro-environment Democratic senators like Sheldon Whitehouse from Rhode Island. The legislation would ease development for renewable energy and transmission lines, but environmental organizations warn it will also fast-track fossil fuels by undermining environmental regulations. “A technology-neutral fast track in the hands of an administration openly hostile to clean energy is not a bargain. It is a one-way ratchet for fossil fuels,” Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement. Currently, new U.S. infrastructure projects must comply with bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). If BAAJA becomes law, those environmental hurdles will become easier to clear. Fewer projects would require NEPA review, the time frame for environmental assessments would be shorter, and the window to sue over approved projects would shrink. Consultation on potential impacts to endangered species would also be shortened. Proponents of the bill say those changes would ease renewable energy development and lower U.S. carbon emissions. “BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change,” Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, wrote on social media. “The bill lowers emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040.” However, the weakened environmental review would also apply…
items.t: US bill to speed up clean energy projects could also fast-track fossil fuels

items.title: This Couple Fostered A Severely Overweight Beagle And Helped Her Rediscover The Joy Of Being A Dog
items.summary:
Autumn the Beagle arrived at her foster home in January 2026 weighing a staggering 72 pounds (32.7 kg). But carrying all that extra weight was far from the only challenge the Beagle was facing. After her previous owner passed away, Autumn was surrendered to a shelter, where she was just one day away from being euthanized. Fortunately, Triangle Beagle Rescue stepped in and reached out to Tricia and Dave, an experienced foster family willing to give Autumn a second chance.

What followed were months of carefully managed meals, veterinary care, short walks, and plenty of patience as the couple helped the sweet Beagle regain her mobility and improve her quality of life. With every pound she shed, Autumn rediscovered some of the simple pleasures of being a dog. Walks became more exciting, playtime became possible again, and the once severely overweight pup grew increasingly comfortable around her foster family. However, some of the most meaningful milestones in her journey had little to do with the number on the scale. Today, Autumn, now known as Daisy Autumn, weighs just 33 pounds (15 kg) and has found a loving forever home where she shares her days with three canine siblings and a family that spoils her.

Bored Panda reached out to Tricia, one of Autumn’s foster parents, to learn more about the weight-loss journey and the challenges of caring for her. Scroll down to discover Autumn’s remarkable transformation and read what Tricia shared with us about her journey.

More info: Instagram 

When Autumn arrived at her foster home, she weighed a staggering 72 pounds…
items.t: Beagle Who Was Just One Day Away From Being Euthanized Loses 39 Pounds And Finds A Loving Home

items.title: Tequila’s hangover: How the drink’s success drove deforestation in Mexico
items.summary: For decades, Manuel García Castro has grown corn, squash and beans to feed his family and livestock. In 2019, he followed in the footsteps of prosperous local farmers and dedicated a portion of his land in the highlands of Jalisco, western Mexico, to planting blue agave, used to make tequila. A friend persuaded him to plant 15,000 shoots on 3 hectares (7.41 acres) of his land and in other areas where his cattle grazed. García Castro would provide the labor; his friend, the capital. “We have to give it a shot to see if there’s some way to make money from something else,” was their thinking, he told Mongabay. Back then, raising livestock didn’t bring in much money and expenses were high. They invested 500,000 Mexican pesos (around $25,300) in plants, pesticides and fertilizers, not including payment for García Castro’s own labor and that of the farm worker who helped him. Four years later, in 2023, hopes of selling the blue agave began to fade. Sale prices per kilogram plunged by as much as 92% compared with those between 2017 and 2019. The business was no longer profitable in the short term. Manuel García and his partner abandoned the fields two years ago. The tequila boom Tequila has a protected designation of origin in the states of Guanajuato, Nayarit, Tamaulipas, Michoacán and Jalisco. The drink is considered a national brand and a symbol of Mexican identity. Over the past decade, the tequila industry has boosted its exports and developed premium…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Tequila’s hangover: How the drink’s success drove deforestation in Mexico

items.title: Chimps In A Remote Tanzanian Forest Stun Scientists By Fishing For Termites With Homemade Tools
items.summary:
Picture a fishing trip where the rod is a blade of grass, the pond is a termite mound, and the catch is a crunchy, protein-rich snack. For a group of chimpanzees in southern Tanzania, that’s just lunch, and scientists have now confirmed they’re doing it farther south than anyone has ever recorded.

Researchers working in Tanzania’s Loasi Forest Reserve found chimps using stripped pieces of grass and bark to pull termites from their mounds. The Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) announced the findings on Wednesday, November 18. Among the evidence was a termite mound still littered with fishing tools the chimps had recently abandoned, left behind after what was presumably a successful meal. 

Scientists in Tanzania’s Loasi Forest Reserve discover wild chimps using grass and bark to fish for termites 

Amani Allan/Pexels 

Termite fishing itself is nothing new to science. Jane Goodall famously watched chimpanzees do it at Gombe, also in Tanzania, in the 1960s, and the observation helped change how scientists define tool use. What makes the Loasi discovery remarkable is the location. These chimps live near the southernmost edge of their species’ entire range, and the finding moves the known southern limit of chimpanzee tool use roughly 143 miles (about 230 km) beyond where it had previously been documented. 

The discovery extends the known southern limit of chimpanzee tool use by roughly 143 miles (about 230 km) 

Francesco Ungaro/Pexels 

The method is simple but effective. A chimp picks a slender piece of plant material, sometimes trimming it to the right shape, and slides…
items.t: Chimps In A Remote Tanzanian Forest Stun Scientists By Fishing For Termites With Homemade Tools

items.title: Relearning how to live with wolves in Europe
items.summary: Across much of Europe, gray wolves were hunted to near extinction by the mid-20th century. In the past couple of decades, though, strict protections have helped the population rebound in some countries. The return of the gray wolf (Canis lupus) has posed a conundrum. Conservation groups view it as a conservation success. However, wolves sometimes kill livestock, which brings them into conflict with some farmers. In response, the European Union recently weakened the wolf protections, making it easier to hunt the animals.  In a conversation with Mongabay’s Mike DiGirolamo, social scientist Emu-Felicitas Ostermann-Miyashita, from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology, argues the situation shouldn’t be seen as wolves versus livestock, but rather “livestock with wolves.”  “Looking back to the point when wolves were abundant in the landscape, it has always been livestock with wolves because people had no other choice,” Ostermann-Miyashita says in the Newscast episode. “And that’s why in the countries where there has been persistent wolf populations without them being exterminated … these protection measures are intact, like fencing or putting the sheep into enclosures during the evening to prevent livestock predation.” By contrast, landscapes where wolves have been extinct for decades or centuries have become more populated with humans who have become habituated to living without wolves, Ostermann-Miyashita says. So the knowledge of how to protect livestock from large carnivores has also been lost, she adds.  Ostermann-Miyashita has studied the conflict between…
items.t: Relearning how to live with wolves in Europe

items.title: US gains foothold in race for Africa’s critical minerals in Kenya’s Mrima Hill project
items.summary: Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Mining and Blue Economy has announced that the mining ministry has issued a “notice of intention” to award the tender for the development of the Mrima Hill mining project to U.S.-based mining consortium Frontier Minerals. Mrima Hill is thought to be rich in critical minerals sought after by electronics, aerospace and energy industries, “The choice of an American consortium reflects a commitment from the Kenyan government to develop their mining sector in a transparent manner that will bring market-leading innovation to Kenya, ensure local value addition, and create jobs and economic benefits [for the U.S. and Kenya],” said the U.S. State Department in a statement. The U.S.’s interest in Kenya’s critical minerals is part of Washington’s effort to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the critical minerals market. According to Kenya’s Ministry of Mining, Mrima Hill holds at least 5.8 million tons of material that may contain niobium pentoxide, which is used to make niobium, a critical element used in electronics, the aerospace industry and energy storage. Two-thirds of the world’s niobium reserves are currently held by Brazil; the remaining third are mostly held by China. The region is also potentially home to millions of metric tons of rare earth elements (REEs), which are key components in the manufacture of batteries, magnets, mobile phones and cars. While in its statement, the U.S. State Department emphasized transparency in the mining sector, Kenyan civil society organizations raised concerns that the…
items.t: US gains foothold in race for Africa’s critical minerals in Kenya’s Mrima Hill project

items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
items.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.
items.t: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

items.title: This Rare Horse With A Playful Personality Is Helping Preserve America’s Living History
items.summary:
When a Cleveland Bay foal named Moose was born in Williamsburg, Virginia, in 2019, his arrival marked an important milestone in the efforts to preserve one of the world’s rarest horse breeds. With his friendly nature, curious personality, and eagerness to interact with people, Moose has since taken on another important role: helping visitors discover a living piece of American history.

Moose was born as part of Colonial Williamsburg’s Rare Breeds Program, which preserves the heritage breeds that played an important role in shaping America. The nonprofit operates a living history museum where visitors can experience life in an 18th-century American town, complete with historic buildings, traditional trades, costumed interpreters, and even the animals that were part of everyday life centuries ago.

Scroll down to see more of Moose and learn about how he’s fulfilling his duties.

More info: colonialwilliamsburg.org | Instagram | Facebook | x.com 

Moose’s large, floppy ears earned him the name shortly after he was born 

Colonial Williamsburg 

Among these animals are Cleveland Bay horses, a breed that originated in England and was once valued for its strength, temperament, and versatility. From pulling carriages and transporting goods to working on farms, these horses served many purposes in early America. However, as machinery and motorized vehicles gradually replaced working horses, their numbers declined dramatically, leaving the breed critically endangered.

Moose was Colonial Williamsburg’s first foal born through a successful embryo transfer…
items.t: Meet The Charming Horse Helping Save A Breed That Once Played A Vital Role In American Life

items.title: International marine biodiversity conference emphasizes the unsung and the unknown
items.summary: BRUGES, Belgium — More than 800 people gathered for the 7th World Conference on Marine Biodiversity, held Nov. 17-20, in Bruges, Belgium. The conference took on topics as varied as deep-sea mining impacts, ocean-related art, citizen science, methods for working with large datasets, environmental DNA and taxonomy. Yet it also raised broader questions about how people value the ocean and whether current approaches serve the health of marine ecosystems. David Obura, founder of Kenyan marine research nonprofit CORDIO East Africa, gave the opening keynote, calling for a shift in thinking about how people use the sea. “If we just use the same values that have historically driven current markets to maximise further benefits from oceans … we just drive oceans farther into decline,” Obura told Mongabay in an email recapping his talk. “We’ve seen this already. Instead we need to apply values that prioritise balance and sustainability across multiple co-benefits, and deliver long term security and prosperity over short term gain.” Many participants emphasized the need to catalog the world’s marine biodiversity and draw attention to overlooked species or those not yet described. “We want to see how many species are there because we want to know what we need to conserve,” Bert Hoeksema, a guest researcher at Naturalis Biodiversity Center, a museum in the Netherlands, told Mongabay. Hoeksema has studied corals for more than four decades and recently published a paper identifying key countries involved in the marine aquarium trade. “There are so many species that are not known.”…
items.t: International marine biodiversity conference emphasizes the unsung and the unknown

items.title: How Uttarakhand’s women farmers are reviving endangered Himalayan medicinal plants
items.summary: RAMNI, Uttarakhand, India — At state fairs across Uttarakhand, while most farmers set up stalls featuring local millet varieties, Guddi Devi and her fellow farmers showcase saplings of high-altitude medicinal plants. “In the past, people used to bring kutki [Picrorhiza kurroa] and other herbs like sugandha bala [Valeriana jatamansi] from the bugyals [alpine meadows]. Since everyone was going there, digging and harvesting, everything was becoming extinct in the alpine meadows. It is a cumbersome task to even reach there, so you won’t easily find [these herbs] there anymore,”  Guddi said. Situated in the Indian Himalayan region, Uttarakhand’s medicinal plants, growing at 2,000 meters (6,500 feet) or more, are highly sought after. Traditionally, locals traveled up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) on foot to collect herbs like kutki — widely used to bring down fevers — when access to medical care was scarce. Globally, market demand for medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) has grown substantially, with $4.2 billion in exports in 2023, and due to unsustainable harvesting practices and overexploitation, many species are at risk. With growing concern, scientists say controlled agricultural cultivation can be a sustainable method to meet the pharmaceutical demands for these plants. “Uttarakhand has diverse agro-climatic conditions, therefore, mountain villages located at about 2500 to 3000 m altitude are suitable locations for domestication or for cultivation of high altitude medicinal and aromatic plants,” known as MAPs, Chandra P. Kuniyal, a scientist at the Herbal Research and…
items.t: How Uttarakhand’s women farmers are reviving endangered Himalayan medicinal plants

items.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.
items.t: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

items.title: The night watchmen guarding Malaysia’s critically endangered river terrapins
items.summary: KEMAMAN, Malaysia — As night settles over Kampung Pasir Gajah, a small team of men can be found sitting in the moonlight by the riverbank. They scroll on their phones, share a late meal, but their ears are tuned to the river. These men call themselves the Terrapin Guardians, or Geng Tuntung in Malay, after tuntung, the local word for river turtles. During nesting season from January to March, they work nights from 10 p.m. until dawn along this stretch of river in Terengganu state, on the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia. They scan for tracks of a heavy shell on the sand — a sign that a southern river terrapin (Batagur affinis) has crawled out of the water to nest. Samsul bin Hamid, 52, a factory production line worker, was once among the villagers who gathered by these riverbanks to harvest terrapin eggs as a seasonal delicacy. He stopped after learning more about the species through the Turtle Conservation Society of Malaysia (TCS). “I learned the ways to track terrapins through friends. Back then, they would invite me to go egg collecting, and I would go. It’s just something we learned being part of the village,” he says. Today, Samsul is one of 13 guardians, all of whom once harvested eggs and now work with TCS to secure nests before natural threats and other collectors find them. According to TCS data, the guardians have collected and incubated 13,224 eggs, and successfully released more than 8,200 young terrapins back into…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: The night watchmen guarding Malaysia’s critically endangered river terrapins

items.title: Brazil’s President Lula moves to recognize Chief Raoni’s Indigenous land
items.summary: Brazil has taken a step toward formally recognizing the Indigenous land where one of the Amazon rainforest’s best-known defenders, Indigenous leader Raoni Metuktire, was born. The Mẽbêngôkre, or Kayapó, and Yudjá, or Juruna, peoples live on the 362,000-hectare (895,000-acre) Kapôt Nhĩnore Indigenous Territory, on the border between Pará and Mato Grosso states in the southern Brazilian Amazon. They have been fighting for legal rights to their land since 2004. On Nov. 19, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, announced in a ceremony a government order that recognizes the two peoples’ permanent right to the territory. For full legal recognition, the territory still needs its borders marked on the ground, final approval by presidential decree and official registration. Only then can authorities remove non-Indigenous occupants. “Today, I had the opportunity to meet again with Chief Raoni, a historic leader of the Indigenous peoples, for whom I have deep respect and admiration,” Lula wrote in an Instagram post, following a visit to the leader. “I also signed the ordinance that recognizes the permanent possession of the Mebêngôkre and Yudjá peoples over the Kapôt Nhinore Indigenous Territory … an important step in guaranteeing the rights of the original peoples,” he said. Raoni has been in palliative care since he was diagnosed with cancer at age 94 earlier in 2026. He was born in the Kapôt Nhĩnore Indigenous Territory, where his father, Umoro, is buried. About 83% of the territory still has its original forest, according to data from Brazil’s Indigenous…This…
items.t: Brazil’s President Lula moves to recognize Chief Raoni’s Indigenous land

items.title: Kenyan communities take on Nigerian billionaire’s $16 billion refinery project as court adjourns hearing
items.summary: Around 40 community representatives gathered early in the morning on Nov. 24 at a county assembly hall in Lamu, a town on an island off Kenya’s coast, to virtually witness a court hearing. The case pits residents against the Dangote group, owned by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote. The conglomerate plans to build an oil refinery on lands where the residents claim they have lived for generations. With an estimated cost of $16 billion and a reported production capacity of 700,000 barrels per day, the East Africa Petroleum Refinery, if it goes ahead, would be the largest in Africa. However, some residents appear not to have been informed of the project beforehand. Because they do not hold formal land title deeds, the government is asking them to leave, the community representatives said. “We want information,” Mzee Hilal Suleiman Ali, an elder from the indigenous Mvinjeni community who attended the hearing, told Mongabay. “We are not opposed to the project, but we want to be included, and above all, we want to keep our land.” On Sept. 30, Dangote held a groundbreaking ceremony attended by several African heads of state. The November hearing was held at the Environment and Land Court in Malindi, around 200 kilometers (125 miles) from Lamu along the Kenyan coast. Because traveling to attend in person would be too expensive, the communities witnessed the proceedings remotely using a phone. Their lawyer, who was present with them, participated in the hearing virtually. After several hours, the judge announced an…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Kenyan communities take on Nigerian billionaire’s $16 billion refinery project as court adjourns hearing

items.title: Despite heavy rains, farmers hope for a viable waterleaf harvest in Nigeria
items.summary: This is Part 2 in a two-part series on Nigerian waterleaf. Read Part 1 here. Except for the occasional roar of an airplane landing on the runway, it’s all quiet and lonely in the plantations surrounding the local airport in Calabar, southeastern Nigeria. Across the vast fields are strips of farmland studded with waterleaf crops grown by women farmers who depend on these crops for their livelihoods. Once harvested, these waterleaf plants are stuffed into large bags and ferried to local markets. But few of these crops have survived the relentless bursts of rain across Nigeria since June. As the rain continues for days on end, many stems become brittle and die shortly afterward. Others become shriveled, with wilting, yellowed leaves thirsting for sunlight. Left: Preparing crops for market. Right: Crop damage, stem cuttings shriveled from excessive rainfall. Images by Kingsley Charles. Among Nigeria’s most-consumed vegetables, waterleaf (Talinum fruticosum) is cherished for its culinary and therapeutic benefits. In southeastern Nigeria, it forms a key ingredient in staple sauces like afang and edikang ikong. Afang soup is made from Gnetum africanum and waterleaf. Image by Kingsley Charles. In September, Mongabay fellow and Nigerian journalist Kingsley Charles began covering the slump. He visited waterleaf farms and local markets across Calabar, where he spoke to dozens of farmers as well as consumers and vendors. Top: Farmer Martina Usang setting manure out in the sun’s heat. Bottom left: Heaps of bags containing decomposed manure on a farm in Calabar. Bottom right: Mature…
items.t: Despite heavy rains, farmers hope for a viable waterleaf harvest in Nigeria

items.title: Nations hail new shark finning rules in the Atlantic. Conservationists say Japan blocked better ones
items.summary: VILAMOURA, Portugal — Shark finning entails slashing fins off sharks and dumping the bodies into the sea, often while they’re still alive. In the Atlantic Ocean, the practice has been banned on paper since 2004, yet some Japanese and Chinese vessels still do it. The fins end up in shark fin soup, a delicacy in parts of Asia, and the bodies sink to the bottom of the sea. The most effective rule to enforce finning bans, called “fins naturally attached,” prohibits vessels from landing fins unattached from bodies. At the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), a multilateral body that governs much of the fishing in the Atlantic and adjacent seas, it’s been proposed 18 years in a row, including in 2026. It’s never passed due largely to resistance from Japan. However, at ICCAT’s recent annual meeting, held Nov. 16-23 in Vilamoura, Portugal, delegates reached a compromise. ICCAT parties, which include 56 countries and the EU, adopted a measure that could establish a fins-naturally-attached rule by 2029 or 2030, under certain conditions, but for the time being allows alternatives for sharks landed frozen, which many are. The deal drew mixed reactions from parties and NGO observers who had backed a straightforward, no-alternatives policy as the best way to end finning, a practice many people regard as cruel and wasteful. “Until we see a no-exceptions rule, we’re not going to be opening the champagne bottle,” Nicolas Blanc, executive co-director of the Portugal-based NGO Sciaena, told Mongabay. The shark finning…This article was originally…
items.t: Nations hail new shark finning rules in the Atlantic. Conservationists say Japan blocked better ones

items.title: As Indonesia burns, communities look to fire-free agriculture for relief
items.summary: In Kalimantan, the Indonesian portion of the island of Borneo, rain is bringing relief to the months-long fire season. Around 684,000 hectares (1.69 million acres) of land burned between January and September, amounting to 36% of the national total, despite the region comprising just 28% of the country’s land area. However, even with the rain, the threat has not completely passed. Satellite data from NASA show many fires continuing to burn in the forests of Kalimantan, while observers told Mongabay fire hotspots have shifted to other, drier areas. This year’s intense fire season has been fueled by the super El Niño weather pattern, which dramatically reduced seasonal rainfall across the country and prompted the dry season to last unusually long — even longer than during the catastrophic fire events of 2015 and 2019. By September, some 12.5 million people in Indonesia had been impacted by fire or smoke, according to the Indonesian Ministry of Health. Katarina Rina, 53, is one of those affected. Rina, a farmer from Hulu Sungai subdistrict in the hills of the Gunung Naning protected forest in Ketapang district, West Kalimantan province, said the level of fire activity was unprecedented in her area. “We have had fires before, but they were quickly controlled, it has never been this bad,” she said in a video interview with Mongabay. “This time the fires spread into the forests and farmland. It was very traumatizing.” Rina told Mongabay her jengkol (dog fruit) garden was “completely burned,” which is a “big loss”…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: As Indonesia burns, communities look to fire-free agriculture for relief

items.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
items.summary:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and…
items.t: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot

items.title: Country diary: Stalked by a herd of ghostly white deer | Mary Montague
items.summary:
Parkanaur Forest Park, County Tyrone: The autumn rut is over, and I meet the eye of a patriarch male as it surveys his extended family

Emerging from a dip in the hillside, the deer’s antlers crown a white head that nods with the stilted grace of his stride. Through the oak trees, he meets my gaze. A raven kroks. I blink. Then the fallow buck’s ghostly form strolls on over the rise.

White deer are a potent symbol across cultures. Celtic mythology interpreted them as messengers from the “Otherworld”. Medieval legend tells of how a white hart (buck or stag) drew Camelot’s King Arthur into the dark…
items.t: Country diary: Stalked by a herd of ghostly white deer | Mary Montague

items.title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
items.summary:
The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead

Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses (Letters, 15 November), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence.

Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles.

Continue reading...
items.t: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters

items.title: This Artist Was Getting Anxious From The News, So He Started Illustrating The Good Stories Instead (30 Pics)
items.summary:
Back in 2018, Italian illustrator Mauro Gatti noticed that the steady stream of grim headlines was making him anxious. Instead of tuning out, the Emmy-winning creative director (the award came for his work on the children’s series StoryBots) went looking for the stories that rarely make the front page. That search became The Happy Broadcast, a project he created to counter the culture of hate and fear with fact-checked, “anxiety-free” news from around the world. 

Every post pairs a real story with one of Gatti’s signature drawings: simple, round-faced characters and cheerful creatures set against bold, bright backgrounds. The formula clearly works. The Instagram page now has over 807,000 followers and more than 1,500 posts. The idea has also grown into a TikTok account, a 2020 book and WHOLE, a mental wellness app the artist runs with his business partner Keith Bonnici. 

Animal rights were among the topics Gatti wanted to see covered from the start, and his book even features a cuddle club that pairs senior dogs with elderly people. For this collection, we’ve picked 30 animal-related illustrations from The Happy Broadcast. They range from new laws protecting cats and dogs to daring rescues, progress in veterinary care and lost pets making their way home. Scroll down to see what’s been going right for animals lately, and follow The Happy Broadcast on Instagram if you’d like more of this kind of news between the usual headlines. 

More info: Instagram | Facebook 

#1 A recent analysis published by the European Respiratory Society suggests that infants who grow up around…
items.t: 30 Times “The Happy Broadcast” Shared Good News About Animals That Might Restore Your Hope In People

items.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
items.summary:
Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines

An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature.

John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under.

items.t: Outcry grows over UK plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules

items.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
items.summary:
The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out

Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF).

“Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.”

‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest

items.title: 33 Of The Most Memorable Rescues By This Brazilian Lieutenant, From Orphaned Anteaters To Strays
items.summary:
As a 33-year-old officer with the Environmental Military Police in Minas Gerais, Brazil, Lieutenant Bernardo Bax spends his days shutting down illegal gold mines, enforcing fishing bans and going after people who keep wild birds in cages. But the side of his work that has won him more than 440,000 followers on Instagram, is much gentler: four baby toucans perched in his lap, a tiny owlet he named Fernanda, and a macaw that couldn’t stop playing with his mustache.

The clip that made many people fall for him shows a baby anteater orphaned after its mother was hit by a car. Instead of waiting in a transport box, the little one crawled inside Bax’s tactical vest, curled up against his chest and took a nap, as if it had decided a police officer would do just fine as a replacement parent. The cute moments are only half of what keeps viewers coming back. The lieutenant uses each rescue to teach something, from why the anteater wanted to cling to him to what you should do if you find a chick that has fallen from its nest.

items.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
items.summary:
Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction

The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all (UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November).

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

Continue reading...
items.t: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter

items.title: Talk of scrapping Natural England smacks of a government not joining the dots
items.summary:
Environmentalists say abolishing independent body will make it easier for landowners and developers ‘to trash nature’

Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.

Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.

Continue reading...
items.t: Abolishing Natural England would be travesty, say campaigners

items.title: Conservationists Bring Kiwi Back To New Zealand’s Capital, And The Birds Are Thriving
items.summary:
For around 150 years, the hills surrounding Wellington, New Zealand, were missing one very special sound: the call of a wild kiwi. These unusual birds, among the country’s most recognizable national symbols, disappeared from the area generations ago. But now, thanks to an ambitious conservation effort, they’re finally making a comeback.

Behind this success is the Capital Kiwi Project, founded by conservationist Paul Ward. Through years of predator control and cooperation with local communities, the project has helped bring kiwi back to the wild landscapes surrounding New Zealand’s capital, where the birds are once again living and breeding freely.

Scroll down to check out how the project moved along and read more about how it got to the point of reinstating a beloved native species.

More info: capitalkiwi.co.nz | Instagram | Facebook | youtube.com 

Before kiwi could return to Wellington’s hills, the Capital Kiwi Project had to tackle one of the biggest threats to their survival: introduced predators 

Capital Kiwi Project 

Trap deployment, Pipinui Point, 2019

Photo by Josiah Watson

Kiwi are unlike most other birds. They’re flightless, mostly nocturnal, and covered in hair-like feathers. They also have long, sensitive beaks with nostrils near the tips, allowing them to sniff out insects, worms, and other food beneath the ground. Found naturally only in New Zealand, these curious-looking birds are also deeply connected to the country’s cultural identity.

items.title: How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar
items.summary:
The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country

As Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold.

“I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.”

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
items.t: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

items.title: 31 Cat And Food Comparisons That Are A Little Too Spot-On (New Pics)
items.summary:
Cat owners have a name for the pose where the paws vanish, and a cat settles into a neat, rounded block: the loaf. 

It’s a fair description, and once you start seeing food in your pets, it’s hard to stop. A curled-up ginger becomes a cinnamon roll. A Siamese with dark ears and paws could pass for a toasted marshmallow. A tabby stretched along the sofa has the stripes of a sausage fresh off the grill.

Spotting these lookalikes is the whole idea behind the Instagram page Soft Cat Memes, which pairs photos of cats with foods they could easily be confused with.

We featured their first collection  a while ago, and there was no shortage of new ones to choose from. This time, you’ll meet fluffy kittens that resemble ice cream sandwiches and chunky gingers in the exact shade of a chicken nugget.

If that is your kind of humor, there are plenty of more funny memes to scroll through.

items.title: ‘Once installed, there’s no getting rid of it’: what Falklands oil plans mean for its seals, whales and penguins
items.summary:
While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems

From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip.

The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.

items.title: Country diary 1906: Peace reigns again in the deer park
items.summary:
28 November 1906: A month ago the hart roared a deep challenge; now he does not threaten but trots with dignity towards his harem

What a difference a few weeks make to the behaviour of the park stags. A month ago, if approached, the excited hart angrily scraped the ground, swelled his shaggy neck, and, lowering his head, coughed defiance or roared that deep, far-sounding challenge. One felt it wise to give him antler-room and leave him to guard his more nervous hinds. Now, though the great beasts are not so timid as the fallow bucks, he does not threaten, but, standing at gaze, waits until we come near; then, wheeling, he trots with dignity towards his harem, turning occasionally to see if we are following. When we have passed he calmly turns his attention once more to the rough park grass. The hinds are won and the annual battles are over; even the silly fellows have ceased to grunt and run aimlessly amongst the trees; peace reigns in the park until next autumn.

An interesting hedgehog story has been sent to me. At a country house near Malvern the cats are fed out of doors from a large dish. Regularly a wild hedgehog comes to the dish and feeds, unmolested by the cats; probably the well-fed cats look upon the hedgehog as an inhabitant of the garden and not as game. This is curious, but not so strange when we consider what a well-armed animal the hedgehog is. Last week, however, the hedgehog brought with it to the dish a young one, but the cats, probably because they were used to the presence of the mother, did not attack the toothsome…

items.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
items.summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.
